best_season: Late summer into autumn. The first ascent was made in October, which on this mountain is the driest and most stable part of the year, though the days are short and the first snows arrive at summit level. July through September gives more daylight and warmer rock. As with everything on Baring, wait for a genuine multi-day dry spell — the gneiss holds water in its vegetated cracks and ledges long after a storm. An east aspect at least catches early morning sun, which helps it dry faster than the north face.

Late June through September. Peak season is July through late August when the approach is snow-free and weather most stable. June approach may encounter residual snow but is feasible. September becomes viable with warmer days but increasing afternoon thunderstorm potential. Winter ascents possible via Silver Star Creek drainage approach for experienced parties; avalanche risk requires careful assessment via NWAC forecasts.

July and early August offer the best conditions. Early July may have lingering snow and wider bergschrunds; late August risks deteriorating weather and warming patterns. Peak climbing window: July 15-August 15. Bluebird weather most reliable mid-July to early August. Route is rarely done outside July-August due to snow and glacier conditions.

approach: From the North Fork Sauk River / Quartz Creek Trailhead (Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie NF, Darrington Ranger District), follow the Quartz Creek Trail about 4 miles, gaining roughly 1,450 ft, to Curry Gap (~4,000 ft) at the Bald Eagle Mountain Trail junction. From Curry Gap head west/southwest along an up-and-down ridge toward Kyes, leaving the ridge where feasible to cross the Pride Glacier west-northwest toward the cliffs below Monte Cristo Peak, reaching the northeast base of Kyes around 6,000 ft.

approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north to Burlington, then WA-20 east through Marblemount, and turn onto Cascade River Road, following its paved-then-gravel surface about 21.7 miles to a small pullout at 3,200 ft that marks the unmaintained Boston Basin Trailhead (a different, lower stop than the Eldorado trailhead a mile or so up-road, and just before the road's end at Cascade Pass). From there a steep, unmaintained climbers' path follows the old Diamond Mine roadbed briefly before climbing hard, crossing several streams, and breaking above treeline (~5,300 ft) to reach the popular Boston Basin high camp around 6,400 ft — roughly 3-4 miles one-way with about 3,000-3,300 ft of elevation gain. From camp, West Ridge climbers continue cross-country over the glacier to a couloir that gains the ridge crest. Because Boston Basin is a high-demand cross-country camping zone in North Cascades National Park, overnight parties need a wilderness permit; a portion of peak-season (mid-May to mid-October) slots can be reserved in advance via Recreation.gov's early-access lottery, with the remainder issued as limited first-come, first-served walk-up permits. For this specific route: from Boston Basin high camp, a short approach up into the Forbidden Peak zone reaches this minor summit; North and South Ridge differ only in which side of the formation is climbed from the same camp.

best_season: July and August offer the most stable and driest weather conditions in the North Cascades, with temperatures averaging 63-70°F during the day and 41-45°F at night. June sees slightly more precipitation (2.2 inches) while July-August drops to 1.7 inches. Occasional afternoon thunderstorms and rapid weather changes are always a possibility at this remote alpine location. Early season (June) can have more heavily crevassed glaciers, while late summer (August-September) offers better snow bridge conditions.
hazards: Exposed granite climbing on remote face with significant consequences for falls
Glacier travel on Chickamin Glacier with crevasse rescue required if roped team breaks through
Severe altitude and remote location (50+ miles from nearest road) means helicopter rescue unlikely
Rapid onset afternoon thunderstorms common in July; exposure to lightning hazard above treeline
Bivouacking in sub-zero temperatures at 8,500 feet with minimal shelter options
Approach trail washouts have occurred (2025-2026); access may be seasonally restricted

best_season: Best as a snow and mixed climb from roughly December through April, once the gully has filled in and consolidated - which is exactly when avalanche hazard has to be managed carefully, since this is a south-facing gully directly below cliffs and adjacent to active ski-area terrain. The NWAC forecast for Snoqualmie Pass is a mandatory pre-trip read; do not climb this on a rising danger day or after significant new loading. Firm winter snow makes the approach and the climbing far faster than soft spring corn. From June through October the same feature is climbed dry as an easy-fifth-class scramble, which is a completely different and much lower-consequence outing.
